passages.happening:
Jacob looks up and sees Esau coming with four hundred men (verse 1). He divides the children among their mothers. He puts the servant women and their children in front, Leah and her children next, “and Rachel and Joseph at the rear” (verse 2).

“But Jacob himself went on ahead and bowed to the ground seven times as he approached his brother” (verse 3).

“Esau, however, ran to him and embraced him, threw his arms around his neck, and kissed him. And they both wept” (verse 4).

Esau sees the women and children. “Who are these with you?” Jacob answers, “These are the children God has graciously given your servant” (verse 5). The servant women and their children come and bow, then Leah and her children, then Joseph and Rachel (verses 6-7).
passages.hearers:
Look at how Jacob lines up his family. The servant women and their sons go first, where the danger is greatest. Leah and her sons come next. Rachel and Joseph, the ones he loves most, are safest at the back. Every person in that family could see the order. The favoritism that split Isaac's house is alive in Jacob's. It will bear bitter fruit in the story of Joseph and his brothers.

But then Jacob does something new. He goes ahead of them all. In chapter 32 he sent his gifts and his family ahead of him. Now, limping, he walks in front.

He bows to the ground seven times. Letters from rulers in Canaan to the king of Egypt, found at Amarna in Egypt and written in the 1300s BC, say the writer falls at the king's feet ‘seven times and seven times’. Jacob bows to his brother the way a servant bows to a king.

And Esau runs. Esau, the one who was wronged, the one who swore to kill him, runs to him. He embraces him, falls on his neck, kisses him, and they both weep. The verbs tumble out one after another. Nothing in Jacob's plans prepared for this.

Genesis does not explain the change in Esau. It does not say the gifts did it. Esau has not even accepted them yet. Many readers remember Jacob's prayer, ‘Please deliver me from the hand of my brother Esau’ (32:11), and see God's hand in turning Esau's heart. The text lets Esau be generous in his own right. Twenty years have passed, and the man who once said he would kill his brother now weeps on his neck.

In the old Hebrew manuscripts the word ‘kissed him’ has dots written over it by the scribes. Ancient Jewish teachers argued about what the dots meant. Some said Esau's kiss was not sincere. Others said that at that moment his love was stirred and he kissed Jacob with his whole heart. The story itself gives no hint that Esau was false.
passages.later:
Some readers hear an echo of this scene in Jesus' parable of the lost son, where the father “ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him” (Luke 15:20). In both stories the one who was wronged runs to the one who wronged him. It is an echo of shape, not a quotation, and Luke does not point to Genesis.

Years later Joseph, the son Jacob kept at the back, will weep over the brothers who sold him: “Joseph kissed each of his brothers as he wept over them” (Genesis 45:15).

Proverbs knows how hard this is: “An offended brother is harder to win than a fortified city” (Proverbs 18:19).
passages.asks: The brother who was wronged was the one who ran. Ask whether there is someone who wronged you whom you could run toward, if God gave you the heart for it. Then ask whether there is someone you wronged who might be readier to forgive than you fear.

passages.happening:
“What do you mean by sending this whole company to meet me?” Esau asks. “To find favor in your sight, my lord,” Jacob answers (verse 8).

“I already have plenty, my brother,” Esau replies. “Keep what belongs to you” (verse 9).

Jacob insists. “If I have found favor in your sight, then receive this gift from my hand. For indeed, I have seen your face, and it is like seeing the face of God, since you have received me favorably” (verse 10). “Please accept my gift that was brought to you, because God has been gracious to me and I have all I need” (verse 11). He presses Esau until he accepts.
passages.hearers:
Listen to what each brother calls the other. Jacob says ‘my lord’. Esau says ‘my brother’. Jacob is still speaking as a servant. Esau is speaking as family.

Esau does not want the gift. He has plenty. He came for his brother, not for animals.

Why does Jacob insist? In that world, to accept a gift between people who had quarreled was to accept the peace it offered. If Esau keeps the animals, the matter is settled. Jacob needs him to take them.

Then the most striking line. ‘I have seen your face, and it is like seeing the face of God.’ The night before, at Peniel, Jacob saw God's face and lived (32:30). Now he sees his brother's face, and it is not anger he sees but welcome. To be received by the brother he wronged feels to him like being received by God.

In verse 11 the Hebrew word for ‘gift’ is the word for ‘blessing’. Jacob says, literally, ‘Please take my blessing.’ Twenty years ago he took Esau's blessing by a lie. Now, in his own way, he tries to give a blessing back. ‘God has been gracious to me and I have all I need.’ The grabber has learned to say ‘enough’.
passages.later:
Jesus taught that peace with God and peace with others belong together: “First go and be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:24).

Paul writes that God “reconciled us to Himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:18).

A psalm sings, “how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony” (Psalm 133:1).
passages.asks: Jacob saw God's welcome in his brother's welcome. Ask whose forgiveness has shown you something of God's. Then ask whether your face could show God's welcome to someone who expects to be turned away.

passages.happening:
Esau says, “Let us be on our way, and I will go ahead of you” (verse 12).

Jacob answers that the children are frail and the nursing animals cannot be driven hard. “Please let my lord go ahead of his servant.” He will follow slowly, he says, “until I come to my lord at Seir” (verse 14).

Esau offers to leave some of his men with him. Jacob says, “Why do that? Let me find favor in the sight of my lord” (verse 15).

“So that day Esau started on his way back to Seir” (verse 16). But Jacob goes to Succoth. He builds a house there and shelters for his livestock, which is why the place is called Succoth (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The brothers are reconciled, but they do not live together. Esau offers to travel with Jacob and to leave men with him. Jacob politely says no to both.

He says he will come to Esau in Seir. Then he goes the other way, to Succoth, and the text never tells of him going to Seir.

Readers take this in two ways. Some see the old Jacob still: afraid, not quite trusting his brother, using smooth words to manage him. On this reading the embrace was real, but Jacob's heart has not fully caught up with his new name.

Others read Jacob's words as the polite speech of that world, which neither brother expected to be taken literally. They note that his reasons were true: young children and nursing animals could not keep pace with four hundred men. They add that God had told Jacob to go back to the land of his fathers (31:3), and Seir lay outside it. Abraham and Lot also parted in peace when living together would not work (chapter 13).

The text makes no comment. A reader can hold both: a real reconciliation, and a man still learning to speak plainly.

Reconciliation does not always mean living close. Sometimes peace means two roads, each walked without hatred. These brothers will meet again to bury their father (35:29).

Succoth means ‘shelters’ or ‘booths’, huts made of branches. It lay in the Jordan Valley, east of the river, near where the Jabbok joins it.
passages.later:
Esau and Jacob stand together at their father's grave: “his sons Esau and Jacob buried him” (Genesis 35:29). Later Esau moves away, because “their possessions were too great for them to dwell together” (Genesis 36:7).

Paul writes, “If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone” (Romans 12:18). Hebrews says, “Pursue peace with everyone” (Hebrews 12:14).
passages.asks: Jacob and Esau made peace and then went separate ways. Ask whether there is a relationship where peace is possible but closeness is not, at least for now. Then ask whether you can keep that peace honestly, without pretending and without hatred.

passages.happening:
“After Jacob had come from Paddan-aram, he arrived safely at the city of Shechem in the land of Canaan, and he camped just outside the city” (verse 18).

He buys the plot of ground where he pitched his tent from the sons of Hamor, Shechem's father, “for a hundred pieces of silver” (verse 19).

“There he set up an altar and called it El-Elohe-Israel” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
‘Arrived safely’ can also be read ‘arrived in peace’ or ‘whole’. At Bethel Jacob vowed that if God brought him back ‘safely to my father’s house’, the LORD would be his God (28:21). He is back in the land. God has kept his promise.

Shechem lay in the hill country, in a pass between two mountains, on the main roads through the land. It is where Abraham built his first altar in Canaan (12:6-7). Jacob comes back to where the story of the land began.

Like Abraham, who bought a field for Sarah's grave (chapter 23), Jacob buys a small piece of land. The family still lives as guests in a land held by others, but now it owns one field. The word translated ‘pieces of silver’ is a rare unit whose weight and value are not known.

Then the altar and its name. El-Elohe-Israel means ‘God, the God of Israel’, or ‘God is the God of Israel’. For the first time Jacob uses his new name. At Bethel he said, ‘then the LORD will be my God’. Now he says it with an altar. The God who renamed him is his God.

The land promise itself is set out in the note on Genesis 12:4-9, with the ways Christians read it.

The next chapter shows that arriving home is not the same as being safe. What happens at Shechem will test this family hard.
passages.later:
Joseph's bones were later buried in this very field. Joshua says they “were buried at Shechem in the plot of land that Jacob had purchased from the sons of Hamor” (Joshua 24:32). Joshua gathered the tribes at Shechem to renew their promise to serve the LORD (Joshua 24:1).

John's Gospel sets a meeting by this field. Jesus sits by Jacob's well near “the plot of ground that Jacob had given to his son Joseph” (John 4:5), and a Samaritan woman asks him, “Are You greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well” (John 4:12).
passages.asks: Jacob came home and built an altar that said: this God is my God. Ask whether you have ever said that plainly, in words or in a choice. Then ask what altar, what act of worship, would say it where you are now.
